title: Mastery Challenge: The Middle Ages
objective: After this level you can demonstrate command of The Middle Ages Levels 1–99 across the whole tree.
summary: Questions from across the tree, from Rome's fall in the West to the wider world of 1500. Every question can be corrected.

cards.headline: The Middle Ages Mastery Challenge.
cards.body: Questions from across the whole tree, from Rome’s fall in the West to a world joined by ships and printing presses. Level 1 gave you a thousand years in one frame; now see how well you can fill it. Take your time: every question can be corrected.

cards.headline: The Middle Ages: mastered
learned: Why the Middle Ages have no single end date, as printing, new ideas and ocean voyages remade Europe.
Why the Renaissance, which called the Middle Ages dark, was built from books medieval monks had copied.
What 1492 joined together, and what it cost the Taíno people who already lived there.
Which great powers flourished beyond Europe, from Mali and Great Zimbabwe to the Aztecs and Inca.

questions.prompt: Which pair of dates makes the Middle Ages begin and end with the fall of each half of Rome?

options.label: 410 and 1066
options.rationale: 410 is Britain’s Roman exit; 1066 is too early for the end.

options.label: 527 and 1492
options.rationale: 527 is when Justinian began to rule.

questions.explanation: The West fell in 476; the Roman East, Byzantium, fell with Constantinople in 1453.

questions.prompt: Renaissance humanists called the Middle Ages dark. What irony did Poggio’s book hunts reveal?

options.label: The ancient texts were written in the Middle Ages
options.rationale: They were ancient; monks copied them.

options.label: The humanists could not read Latin
Monasteries refused to lend any books
The classics they loved survived in medieval monks’ copies

questions.explanation: Poggio found Cicero, Quintilian and Lucretius in monastery libraries, copied by medieval monks.

questions.prompt: What did the 1939 dig at Sutton Hoo in Suffolk uncover?

options.label: A Roman fort with its gates intact
options.rationale: It was an Anglo-Saxon ship burial.

options.label: An Anglo-Saxon ship burial full of treasure
A Viking longhouse and its hearth
options.rationale: It was an Anglo-Saxon ship burial.

options.label: A monastery library of 600 books
options.rationale: It was an Anglo-Saxon ship burial.

questions.explanation: Basil Brown found a ship burial, probably King Rædwald’s, with 263 finds including a famous helmet.

questions.prompt: Why did Europe go from thousands of books to more than 9 million by 1500?

options.label: Reusable metal type printed whole editions at once
Monasteries hired many more scribes
Books were imported from China by sea
options.rationale: The change was printing in Europe.

options.label: Parchment became cheap enough to buy

questions.explanation: Movable type let printers run off editions of hundreds or a thousand copies.

questions.prompt: A friend says Columbus proved the Earth was round. What’s the best correction?

options.label: He proved it was flat at the edges
Magellan proved it, not Columbus
Educated Europeans already knew; he got its size wrong
Nobody knew until the 1700s
options.rationale: They knew by the early 7th century.

questions.explanation: Educated Europeans knew Earth was a sphere; Columbus thought it much smaller than it is. The myth comes from Irving’s 1828 book.

questions.prompt: What happened to the Taíno people in the decades after 1492?

options.label: They moved away to South America
They grew in number through trade
They were left alone on the smaller islands
Enslavement, starvation and disease cut them to a few thousand

questions.explanation: From perhaps one or two million, the Taíno were reduced to a few thousand by 1520.

questions.prompt: Why is “richest person ever” for Mansa Musa best called a popular claim?

options.label: His wealth is impossible to calculate accurately
Mali had no gold at all
Al-Umari said he was poor
options.rationale: Al-Umari described lavish gifts of gold.

options.label: Richer kings are named on the Catalan Atlas
options.rationale: The atlas called him the richest.

questions.explanation: Historians say his wealth can’t be measured; there’s no ledger, and gold mines don’t convert neatly to dollars.

questions.prompt: Colonial-era writers credited Great Zimbabwe to the Queen of Sheba or Phoenicians. What did archaeology show?

options.label: It was built by Roman engineers
It was medieval and African, built by Shona ancestors
It was a modern colonial building
It was an Egyptian trading post

questions.explanation: In 1905 and 1929 excavations showed the ruins were medieval and African, built by ancestors of the Shona.

options.label: The Inca capital high in the Andes
The largest city north of Mexico, near modern St. Louis
A Maya city in the Yucatán
The island capital of the Aztecs

questions.explanation: Cahokia, near St. Louis, flourished about 950 to 1350 as the largest city north of Mexico.

questions.prompt: Which type of ship carried Portugal’s explorers down Africa and two of Columbus’s three ships in 1492?

options.label: The longship
The galley
The caravel
The steamship

questions.explanation: The Portuguese developed the caravel for Africa’s coast; the Niña and Pinta were caravels.
